question: Large numbers of exotic animals are being imported into the EU or traded illegally, mostly via online platforms. This trade gives rise to problems, causes suffering for millions of animals that are kept in captivity and transported in inadequate conditions, reduces their population in their natural habitats and (given their zoonotic potential) increases the risk to human health and safety.

Parliament has adopted a resolution on improving EU regulations on wild and exotic animals to be kept as pets in the European Union through an EU positive list listing animals that may be kept as pets and pose no threat to human health. In light of this: Does it intend to establish a common EU legislative framework to regulate the trade in exotic animals?
answer: The EU is well-placed to lead the fight against wildlife trafficking and to help protect endangered species from unsustainable exploitation. EU law (1) on wildlife trade already go beyond the requirements of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES).

The revised EU Action Plan against Wildlife Trafficking (2) further strengthens the ambitions of the 2016 Action Plan and shows the continued dedication of the EU to the fight against wildlife trafficking.

For example, in line with the revised Action Plan, the Commission is carrying out an exploratory study on the need for added value and feasibility of revising existing measures or creating new tools, including, for instance, a science-based EU-wide positive list of species of which specimens taken from the wild could be traded or kept as pets.

As the work on the exploratory study is still ongoing, its outcome and the Commission’s possible further steps, if any, cannot be prejudged. Following an open tender procedure (3), the contract for the study has been awarded at the end of 2023. The study will run until the second half of 2025.

The Commission will continue to implement the action plan in close cooperation with the Member States with a view to facilitating ambitious and comprehensive action and cooperation to put an end to illegal trade in wildlife and to the unsustainable exploitation of endangered species.

Council Regulation (EC) No 338/97 of 9 December 1996 on the protection of species of wild fauna and flora by regulating trade therein, OJ L 61, 3.3.1997, p. 1-69. Commission Regulation (EC) No 865/2006 of 4 May 2006 laying down detailed rules concerning the implementation of Council Regulation (EC) No 338/97 on the protection of species of wild fauna and flora by regulating trade therein, OJ L 166, 19.6.2006, p.

1-69. Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) No 792/2012 of 23 August 2012 laying down rules for the design of permits, certificates and other documents provided for in Council Regulation (EC) No 338/97 on the protection of species of wild fauna and flora by regulating trade therein and amending Commission Regulation (EC) No 865/2006, OJ L 242, 7.9.2012, p. 13-45.

Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/2770 of 12 December 2023 prohibiting the introduction into the Union of specimens of certain species of wild fauna and flora in accordance with Council Regulation (EC) No 338/97 on the protection of species of wild fauna and flora by regulating trade therein, OJ L, 2023/2770, 13.12.2023.
